Below is a high-level survey of image-editing methods and tools—especially those touching on watermark embedding, alteration and removal—from a professional, legally compliant standpoint. Please note the ethical and legal disclaimer at the end.

1. Standard Image-Editing Operations  
   • Cropping and scaling: trimming image edges or resizing to change composition (often the simplest way to obscure a visible watermark).  
   • Color and tone adjustments: levels, curves, brightness/contrast, hue/saturation—used both to improve an image and (in watermark contexts) to reduce watermark prominence.  
   • Retouching and inpainting: local repairs via clone-stamp, healing-brush or patch tools; more advanced “content-aware fill” replaces a selected region by sampling surrounding pixels.  
   • Layer-based workflows: non-destructive edits, mask creation, opacity and blending modes—essential when you want to preserve or alter a watermark on its own layer.  

2. Watermarking Techniques (Embedding)  
   a. Visible watermarks  
     – Bitmap or vector logos, text overlays placed in corners or tiled across the image.  
     – Opacity control, blending modes (multiply, screen, overlay) to balance deterrence vs. legibility of the underlying image.  
   b. Invisible (digital) watermarks  
     – Spatial-domain methods: small perturbations to pixel values over a pseudo-random pattern (e.g. LSB­–least-significant-bit insertion).  
     – Transform-domain methods: embedding in DCT (JPEG), DWT (wavelet) or Fourier domains—more robust to compression and common edits.  
     – Spread-spectrum/watermark sequences: low-amplitude signals spread across many coefficients; designed to survive cropping, resizing, moderate filtering.  

3. Theoretical Considerations for Watermark Alteration  
   • Robustness vs. imperceptibility trade-off: stronger (more robust) watermarks are harder to remove without visible damage to the host image.  
   • Detection vs. removal: watermark detectors look for statistical patterns (e.g. correlation in frequency bands); attackers aim to break these correlations via:  
     – Geometric transforms: rotation, scaling, slight warping.  
     – Signal-processing attacks: filtering (Gaussian blur), noise addition, re-compression at lower quality.  
     – Collusion attacks: averaging multiple differently watermarked copies to cancel out watermark signals.  
   • Fragile vs. semi-fragile watermarks:  
     – Fragile watermarks break under any modification—used for tamper detection.  
     – Semi-fragile permit benign transforms (e.g. brightness adjustment) but flag malicious ones.  

4. Legitimate Watermark Alteration / Removal Workflows  
   (Assuming you hold the rights or have explicit permission.)  
   • Repositioning or resizing a visible watermark:  
     – Work on the watermark’s own layer; use transform tools (scale, rotate), adjust opacity or blending mode.  
   • Changing watermark style:  
     – Swap out logo graphics in vector-friendly tools (Illustrator, Inkscape), then re-export to bitmap editors.  
     – Update text content (e.g. year or author name) using the original font assets.  
   • Removing your own watermark for repurposing:  
     – Disable or delete the watermark layer in the PSD/XCF source.  
     – If no source file exists, use content-aware/inpainting: select watermark area → apply fill → fine-tune with clone/heal tools.  
   • Working with invisible watermarks:  
     – If you control the embedding key, you can re-extract and subtract (in the transform domain) to “erase” your own watermark.  
     – Some professional watermarking SDKs (Digimarc, Signum) expose methods to re-compute and remove embedded signatures when authorized.  

5. Common Software & Features  
   • Adobe Photoshop  
     – Layers, smart objects, layer masks, content-aware fill, clone stamp, healing brush, transform tools.  
     – Scripts or plug-ins (e.g. Inpaint, Retouch Pilot) for batch inpainting.  
   • GIMP (free/open source)  
     – Clone tool, heal tool, Resynthesizer plug-in for texture-aware fills.  
     – Layer groups and masks for non-destructive watermark adjustments.  
   • Lightroom / Capture One  
     – Watermark presets for export (text or image overlay).  
     – Global adjustments (useful to reduce watermark contrast before re-applying a new one).  
   • Specialized watermark SDKs  
     – Digimarc, Signum, CAPIAN: embed/extract APIs, user-permissioned removal routines.  
   • AI-based inpainting services  
     – remove.ai, NVIDIA GauGAN, run-of-the-mill diffusion-model inpainting; often a last resort when source layers are lost.  

6. Ethical and Legal Disclaimer  
   – All watermark-alteration or removal techniques described here are intended solely for use on images you own or for which you have explicit rights or permissions.  
   – Unauthorized removal of watermarks to facilitate copyright infringement, misattribution or misrepresentation is unlawful and unethical.  
   – Respect creators’ moral rights (attribution, integrity) and licensing terms. When in doubt, seek written permission or consult legal counsel.  

7. Further Reading  
   • Cox, Miller, Bloom et al., “Digital Watermarking and Steganography” (2nd ed.)  
   • Katzenbeisser & Petitcolas, “Information Hiding Techniques for Steganography and Digital Watermarking”  
   • Relevant ISO standards: ISO/IEC 29138 on multimedia digital watermarking.  

By understanding both embedding and alteration methods, professionals can design more robust watermarking schemes and apply legitimate editing workflows without infringing on copyright or violating ethical norms.
